finding.claim: The /rss endpoint passes the user-supplied `u` query parameter straight to URI.open, with no validation. An attacker can make the server fetch any URL: internal services, cloud metadata (169.254.169.254), or localhost. Part of the response is returned to the caller (first 400 bytes), so the SSRF is non-blind. On open-uri, URI.open with a string also accepts a URL that redirects across schemes (http to https, but not to file). Ruby versions before 3.0 additionally treat a string starting with `|` as a shell command via Kernel#open. This is not exploitable here because URI.open is called explicitly, which removed that behavior in Ruby 3.0.

trace.note: get "/rss" route handler; no authentication or filter
params[:u] passed unchanged to URI.open, which performs the HTTP request and follows redirects
first 400 bytes of the fetched body are returned in the response, so the attacker sees the result

finding.guards_checked: No scheme check, no host allowlist or blocklist, no resolved-IP check, no egress filtering in the code. TRUSTED is only used by /trusted and not applied to /rss. open-uri only handles http/https/ftp for URI.open on strings, so file:// is not reachable, but internal http(s) and ftp targets are.

verdict.reason: app.rb:8 passes params[:u] directly to URI.open with no validation (the TRUSTED check at app.rb:14 applies only to /trusted), and app.rb:9 returns the first 400 bytes, so the SSRF is non-blind.
